hero.name: Pedro Morago
hero.lede: I test software the way I was taught to do maths.
hero.text: I've spent five years in test automation, first on international SaaS products and now on a telecom platform. At IriusRisk I owned the test strategy for a product module and cut CI pipeline time by 40% with an optimization model I designed.

feature.title: Cutting CI pipeline time by 40%
feature.text: End-to-end tests were split unevenly across parallel CI containers, and the longer the pipeline ran, the more it cost. I built an optimization model in Python that decides which container runs each test file. It needed no extra infrastructure, and the result was validated in production.

link.sr: about cutting CI pipeline time by 40%

items.title: CI Shard Advisor
items.text: I turned the pipeline idea into a public tool. It reads Cypress run reports and recommends how to split the test files across containers so that the slowest one finishes as early as possible. For most inputs nobody knows the right answer in advance, so I test its core with property-based, metamorphic and invariant tests.

items.title: Screen Recorder (QA mode)
items.text: I built this Chrome extension for my own bug reports. It records console logs and network requests along with the video, and saves each step with a Cypress or Playwright selector ready to paste into a test. I test it against a bug bench I built, a page that breaks on demand.

items.title: QA Wiki
items.text: I've written more than 50 articles for my public wiki, on test strategy, API testing, Playwright, CI/CD for QA, performance testing and QA for telecom OSS/BSS. I keep adding to it.

items.title: This site
items.text: It has its own test suite. On every push, the suite checks each page at six screen widths and measures text contrast in light and dark mode. The site deploys only when every check passes.

howITest.title: How I test
howITest.lede: There's a saying in software that perfect is the enemy of good. It always grated on me a little. In maths, where I started, a proof is either right or wrong, and I think that's partly why I ended up in QA.

items.title: I check that it does what it should
items.text: Nobody can prove that software has no bugs. I check each feature against what it's meant to do and automate those checks so problems show up early. At Fieldeas I moved the team from manual testing to automation.

items.title: A bug stays open until I know why
items.text: When something breaks, I keep digging until I understand the cause. I write down what I learn in my QA Wiki.

items.title: My bug reports come with the evidence
items.text: A bug report should give the developer what they need to reproduce the bug. When the screen recorder I used for mine changed, I built my own Chrome extension to capture that evidence.

items.title: I check what AI tells me
items.text: AI tools are part of my work, and I use them carefully. On my wiki, the AI answer button replies only from articles I wrote, and it cites the ones it used.
